content: Similarly, no differences were observed in glucose levels, high-density lipoprotein (HDL), triglycerides (TG), or systolic and diastolic BP between control and intervention groups three years post-intervention (Meyer et al.). Three systematic reviews evaluated the effectiveness of high-intensity interval training (HIIT), resistance training, and school-based physical activity (PA) programs compared to no intervention on cardiometabolic health outcomes. Across all three reviews, interventions were consistently associated with improved cardiometabolic outcomes, though the precision of effect sizes varied, and only a few individual trials demonstrated statistically significant benefits of physical activity across all outcomes. Eddolls et al. (2017) reviewed 13 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 1,899 participants and found that HIIT was associated with improvements in systolic and diastolic BP. However, only two out of five RCTs reporting BP outcomes found these improvements to be statistically significant compared to moderate-intensity training or control groups. Four RCTs examined the effects of HIIT on glucose, total cholesterol, HDL, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), TG, and insulin, with most reporting moderate improvements. Moderate evidence supports the positive association between physical activity and cardiometabolic health in children and adolescents, particularly for plasma TG and insulin levels. Bea et al. Pozuelo-Carrascosa et al. found significant intervention effects on systolic BP, total cholesterol, and fasting glucose in their analysis. However, aerobic training did not significantly affect total cholesterol, HDL, or TG. In boys, LDL levels decreased during the control period prior to the intervention (Rowland et al.). Longitudinal studies and cross-sectional analyses revealed mixed results regarding the association between physical activity and cardiometabolic outcomes. For example, meeting physical activity guidelines was associated with reduced odds of high BP in some studies but showed no effect on pre-high BP or high BP risk in others (de Moraes et al., 2015). Total physical activity was favorably associated with diastolic BP in some studies, while systolic BP associations were mixed, with some studies showing favorable, null, or mixed results. Similarly, triglyceride levels showed favorable associations with total physical activity in some studies, while others reported null or mixed findings. Regarding cholesterol, meeting physical activity guidelines was favorably associated with HDL cholesterol in some studies, while total cholesterol associations were mixed. LDL cholesterol showed no significant associations with physical activity in most studies. Fasting insulin levels were also favorably associated with physical activity in several studies, though mixed results were observed in others. Fasting glucose levels showed favorable associations with total physical activity in some studies, while others reported null or mixed findings. HbA1c levels and inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) generally showed null associations with physical activity. Similarly, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels and arterial properties such as pulse wave velocity (PWV) and carotid intima-media thickness (IMT) showed limited or null associations with physical activity. Overall, the evidence suggests that physical activity, particularly moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA), is positively associated with several cardiometabolic health outcomes in children and adolescents. However, the strength and consistency of these associations vary across studies and outcomes.
